blocks.text: ومنه لنسفعن بالناصية سفع الطاير لطم اي لنجرنه بها الي النار بجناحية وفلان فلانا او لنسودن وجهه او لنعلمنه لطمه وضربه والشي اعلمه علامة اهل النار والسوافع ووسمه والسموم وجهه لفحه لوايح السموم لفحا يسيرا وبناصيته قبض عليها فاجتذ بها [wa-minhu la-nasfaʿanna bi-l-nāṣiya safaʿa al-ṭāyir laṭama ay la-najurrannahu bihā ilā al-nār bi-janāḥiyya wa-fulān fulānan aw la-nusawwidanna wajhahu aw la-nuʿlimannahu laṭamahu wa-ḍarabahu wa-l-shay aʿlamahu ʿalāmat ahl al-nār wa-l-sawāfiʿ wa-wasamahu wa-l-samūm wajhahu lafaḥahu lawāyiḥ al-samūm lafḥan yasīran wa-bi-nāṣiyatihi qabaḍa ʿalayhā fa-ijtadha bihā]. The verb سفع [safaʿa], said of a bird, means: it clapped its wings; it also means: it struck with a sound; [III, 185] and further: it struck with a resounding blow. Also: it branded something with a mark. A pestilential wind is also said to clap, to strike, someone's face, when it scorches him with its heat by a mere blast or touch. Also, with "by the forelocks", it means to seize and drag; as in that passage of the Qur'an (Sur. 96: 15.): truly We shall clap their faces by the forelocks, that is, We shall seize them by the forelocks and drag them to the fire of Gehenna; or, We shall blacken their faces, or brand them with the mark of the damned in the fire. Finally, the winds that scorch and blacken with a pestilential blast are called the clappers (which strike with a hiss). So FIRUZABADI, in Schultens on Proverb. XXIII, 30. p. 305.

Bochart could have added that the root صفع [ṣafaʿa] is also preserved in the Arabic dialect, and that it has the same meaning as سفع [safaʿa], namely to blow upon, to strike with a blast or with a hiss. Thus Amr ibn Kulthum in the Muʿallaqa, describing triple-meshed coats of mail: كان غضونهن متون عدر تصفعها الرياح اذا جرينا [ka-anna ghuḍūnahunna mutūnu ghudrin taṣfaʿuhā al-riyāḥu idhā jarayna] As if their wrinkles were the surfaces of pools which the winds ruffle with their blast when we are urged on at a run. [III, 186] So Schultens, loc. cit. It is clear that the two roots, سفع [safaʿa] and صفع [ṣafaʿa], agree with each other not only in sound but also in meaning, since the first notion of both, to strike, to hit, is transferred first to the burning wind called Samum, when it touches or strikes someone's face with its heat, and then to any burning and harmful blast, such as is attributed to basilisks, which for this reason received the name צפע among the Hebrews. — According to Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 6, p. 2130, the basilisk seems to have received the name צפע from صُوفَعَة [ṣūfaʿa] turban; "for," he says, "it bore something on its head, which the Greeks called horns and so named it κεράτην [keratēn]; others compared it to a crown or diadem and called it regulus, βασιλισκον [basiliskon], recognizing it as the king, as it were, and the most powerful of serpents."
